stem: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition in which the kidneys have which problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Damage or abnormal structure that impairs blood filtering
options.misconception: None — CKD is damage or structural problems that impair filtration.
options.explanation: In CKD the kidneys are damaged or structurally abnormal, so they cannot filter blood the way they should and waste and extra fluid build up.

options.label: B
options.text: A sudden, reversible drop in filtering over days
options.misconception: Confuses the time course of acute kidney injury with chronic kidney disease.
options.explanation: A sudden, often reversible fall in filtration over hours to days is acute kidney injury; CKD is lasting damage that impairs filtering.

options.label: C
options.text: Overproduction of erythropoietin by the renal cortex
options.misconception: Reverses CKD's hormonal effect: failing kidneys make too little erythropoietin.
options.explanation: Damaged kidneys make too little erythropoietin, which is why CKD causes anemia; excess erythropoietin points to a tumor or hypoxic drive instead.

options.label: D
options.text: Overproduction of active vitamin D by tubular cells
options.misconception: Reverses CKD's effect on vitamin D activation.
options.explanation: Diseased kidneys make too little active vitamin D, which contributes to secondary hyperparathyroidism; overproduction is not a feature of CKD.

options.label: E
options.text: Glucose loss in urine from an inherited transporter defect
options.misconception: Equates an isolated tubular transport defect with loss of filtering function.
options.explanation: Inherited glucose loss in urine is familial renal glucosuria, an isolated transporter defect with normal filtration, not CKD.

context: Learning objective: CKD is kidney damage or a structural problem that prevents normal blood filtering, so waste and extra fluid build up.
